notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0530.tlg005.1st1K-gr: 1.1: 'μοναχῶν' (solitaries/monks) is odd in context and may be corrupt. Mantias is presumably the Herophilean physician. 'προαρθρημβολημένου' is corrupt; rendered as 'reduced' (cf. ἐμβεβλημένου). The bandage names σκέπαρνος, σιμός, ὀφθαλμός, ῥόμβος, ἡμίτομον are Hippocratic types (Off. 7); 'half-rhomb' for ἡμίτομον is conventional. 2.1: 'ἀναλκαπρίδες' unidentified, probably corrupt; 'πλωτοί' rendered 'knitted' tentatively. 3.1: 'ὤᾳ' taken as the selvage. 5.1: 'ἀριθμῶν' (numbers) may be corrupt; 'ἀρειάς' read as ἀρετάς; 'δρῆσθαι' at the end presumably for ὁρῆσθαι ('to be seen'), as earlier.

6.1: the opening phrase εὐχρησίας τῶν ἐπιδεομένων is rendered literally; the text in several places of this passage (e.g. ἐληνέειν for ἠπίως/ἐλινύειν, εἶ ἐπιλόγιστος) seems corrupt and was translated by sense. 11.1: ὅπου κεχιέσθαι ἐπὶ γόνει appears corrupt; read as χιασθεῖσαι ἐπὶ γένειον, ‘crossed… to the chin’, uncertain. ὕλῃ in 9.1 read as ὅλῃ. 12.1: καταβαλῶν read as courses (perhaps καταβολῶν).

15.1 (19.1): περιεσκυθισμένων (lit. 'scalped') is unclear in this context; the latter part of the line (σεσημειωμένων etc.) is syntactically obscure and the rendering is tentative. 17.1: κικίνων read as κικίννων ('curls'). 21.1 σπεγκρανίς, 22.1 'masterless Thais', 33–35 φορβέα ('halter'), ἀνεζευγμένος, Γλαυκίου σκάφιον and κέφαλον are names of bandages not otherwise identified; κέφαλον may be corrupt. 25.1: ὑπὸ ἰνίῳ ὠτὸς seems corrupt (perhaps ὑπὸ λοβῷ ὠτὸς). 26.1–27.1: κατ' αὐτούς presumably refers to the sinciput. 29.1: second half is garbled; translated as far as possible. 36.1: μέχρι τοῦ σκεπούσης ὅλης παρειὰς is ungrammatical; sense given. 'Adding the lobe' (ἐπιθεὶς τὸν λοβόν) is unclear.

Line 1: the sense of 'in single combats' (ἐν μονομαχίαις, presumably gladiatorial) is as read; 'the animal' is presumably the hare or some eared creature the bandage resembles. Line 2: the text of the clause on loops (συντόμῳ ... πολλάκις) seems disordered. Several lines are telegraphic and partly corrupt, especially 48 (the final clause on knots and pins), 54 (anacoluthic verbs), and 57 (ἐπισφαίριον, read as ἐπὶ σφαίριον). In 56 'small corner' is the outer corner of the eye. χαλινός is rendered 'corner of the mouth'. σφαίριον is taken as the tip of the nose.

The section headings (bandage names) are absent from the text as given, so some passages lack an explicit subject; 77 is evidently the spica (στάχυς, 'ear of grain'). In 69, λοβοὺς lacks a preposition; 'under' is supplied. In 62 the 'red leather' (δέρματος φοινικίνου) may mean purple-red or palm-coloured leather.

Section titles (names of the individual bandages) are not part of these lines, so references such as 'the one before it' depend on headings absent here. 85.1: 'κατὰ τὸν τοῦ αὐχένας σφόνδυλον' read as αὐχένος. 89.1 'λύκον βρόχον' ('wolf' loop) is obscure. 91.1 περιειλεῖτε/καταλαβοῦ read as imperatives. 100.1, 101.1: 'ἀκίς' (arrowhead) and 'ἀστήρ' (star) are names of other bandages; 101.1 'προσαπόδος κατὰ δύο ἤδη' is unclear, possibly corrupt. 102.1 syntax is broken (accusative προσαποδιδομένην without governing verb). 103.1 'τέτρατον' uncertain. 106.1 'ἁρματηλάται' read as charioteers. Sostratus is presumably the Alexandrian surgeon.

110.1: τόποι is taken as a measure of length (hand-breadths); the sense is uncertain. 111.1: 'leaving another bandage hanging' renders παριέντες ἑτέρου ἐπιδέσμου, whose construction is unclear; the text may be corrupt. The sense of 'it is completed again at the groin' (ἐπιτελεῖται πάλιν βουβῶνι) is also uncertain. 114.1: διὰ δὲ αὐτοῦ ('through this') presumably refers to the slit.

nodes.text: GALEN'S BOOK ON BANDAGES.

It seems to me that it was not without purpose that old Hippocrates, after surveying the other arts, spoke out at the beginning about neatness in practice. 'For my part,' [he says,] 'I am pleased to apply my mind to the whole art: for whatever works it manages well or rightly, one must do each of them well and rightly; whatever [call for] neatness, neatly; and whatever works [call for] speed, quickly. And whatever must be handled painlessly, [one must] do as painlessly as possible. And all other things of this kind one must do differently from one's neighbours, for the better.' For, as it seems, in some works the experienced craftsmen differ from the unskilled who lack the art in nothing else than speed and good rhythm. Therefore it often befits the physician, more than any other craftsman, to aim in all things at doing something well, inasmuch as he also has material that is different. For when cutting and burning, and indeed when bandaging, and if he performs any other operation by hand, he must take thought, along with acting beneficially, for acting neatly and with good rhythm, as he himself again says somewhere: 'Of bandaging there are two kinds: while it is being done, and when it has been done. While it is being done: quickly, painlessly, readily, with good rhythm; quickly, to accomplish the works; painlessly, to act with ease; readily, prepared for everything; with good rhythm, to be pleasant to look at.' For affections arising in certain parts of the body demand the suitable bandaging; and people also often demand, for appearance's sake, good rhythm in bandaging, as in the case of solitaries and all the others who get themselves ready to go out in public. For this reason it is necessary to know the bandagings that suit every part of the body, both simple and elaborate, understanding that both kinds suit some of the parts, while only one, I mean the elaborate one, suits others, even if some think otherwise. But it is worth first settling the dispute. Some have condemned elaborate bandagings as useless, claiming that their use is harmful, employing no sound demonstration but the testimonies of ancient men. First of all they bring in Hippocrates, who says: 'But those who delight in fine bandagings also do a great deal of other damage', that is, in elaborate ones. And they relate of Mantias that, when someone had been bandaged by a drug-seller with an elaborate bandaging on the head and the face, his eyes fell out because of the bandaging. And it seems to them that this also happened for a reason, because the bandages come to bear unevenly on account of the elaborateness, which can bring bodies to inflammations and abscesses. Well then, it is worth recognising that the things they speak of would occur not because of the elaborateness of the bandages, but because of the ineptitude of those using them, who tighten the bandaging. For one must bandage as Hippocrates says: 'In these cases above all, of bandaging: pressure such that the things applied neither stand away nor are pressed very hard, but are fitted, not forced.' And they, bringing in Hippocrates as witness, ought to have given the rest as well. For it was not stated without qualification, 'But those who delight in fine bandagings also do a great deal of other damage', but with the addition 'without sense'. And let them consider, from what is now being said, that Hippocrates does not reject elaborate bandagings. He himself, at any rate, in the book On the Surgery, discussing bandaging and having said what the excellence in bandaging would be, next also speaks thus about the bandaging once displayed: 'well, finely'; putting 'well' for what is beneficial, and 'finely' for what is seemly. Then, to unfold 'finely', he adds: 'finely: simply, distinctly'; putting 'simply' not as applying to every case, but by way of example, as if [to say] let the simple bandaging be distinct. And he makes this clear when he adds: 'either similar and equal parts equally and similarly, or unequal and dissimilar parts unequally and dissimilarly. The kinds [are]: simple, circular, adze, snub, eye, and rhomb, and half-rhomb. The kind [should be] suited to the form and to the affection of those being bandaged.' For if one is simple, it ought in fact to be circular; and if one is adze, it [ought to be] snub. For thus the one that is equal will be like itself throughout, and the unequal [will be] dissimilar. Are they now persuaded, then, that Hippocrates avoids elaborate bandagings, when they agree that the adze, the eye, the rhomb and the half-rhomb are elaborate bandagings? Or shall we further remind them of the account of the fractured collarbone in On Joints, how Hippocrates used the 'crane', which is an elaborate bandaging? Let them know that for certain parts, as for a thigh that has been reduced, the upper arm somewhat, the elbow and many others, it is not possible to use any bandaging other than an elaborate one. But on these matters what has been said is sufficient.

Let us bring the discussion back to the systematic account of bandages and of bandaging. And let us see in what ways bandages differ from one another: in material, form, length, breadth, construction. In material, since some of them are woollen, some linen, some leather, their use being not single nor of the same kind, but varied. For we try to make the choice in use suited to the affection: for whatever requires tightening, we use linen ones on them; but whatever requires not tightening, because it is counter to certain inflammations, but only holding together or covering, woollen ones. And leather ones, as Hippocrates used for a fractured nose and jaw, gluing the end on to what needs bandaging. In form, since some are rolled, some split, others sewn together. Rolled ones, then, are those made from a strip of continuous length without joins, such as those employed for fractures of the limbs. Split ones are those made from a single cloth torn at the ends or in some other part, such as those employed for a head that has been trephined, called 'crabs', four-legged or six-legged or eight-legged. Sewn ones are those put together from several strips, having an application of dissimilar shape, such as those called *analkaprides* or *anazostrai* (girdles) or breast-bands, or those fitting the breasts and the region of the seat. In length, since some are longer, some shorter. And similarly it holds for breadth, both the length and the breadth being fitted proportionally to the parts being bandaged. In construction they differ from one another, since some are woven, some knitted, some plaited. And of the woven ones, some have been made for this purpose, while others come from fabrics made for another use and then torn. These we use for wounds as a rule; those woven for this purpose [we use] as for huntsmen bandaged to protect their legs, and for the so-called wrist-bands. Plaited ones [we use] as for charioteers, for holding the ribs together.

Let it be common to all the precepts on bandaging that [material] be easily obtained, and that one be able to use what is at hand as if it were the best. But when there is a choice, [the rule is] to select the bandages as Hippocrates said. For he says: 'Let the bandages be fine, clean, light, thin, soft, sound, so as to bear stretching and be a little stronger, without seams or loose threads.' They must be clean, because what is dirty is unseemly, and does not take up the moistening liquids, and causes some harm when mixed with the moistening liquids. Let them also be of their own colour, so that it does not come from purple or some other dye, or present to us the appearance of flowing blood or a resemblance to its colour. Thin, so as not to produce too much bulk with the turns. Soft, so as not to squeeze because of hardness. Light, so that the bandaging does not become burdensome from the weight they carry. Let them have no uneven seams either, since these will cause squeezing for that reason, nor loose threads, that is, neither a ragged edge, nor a twist, nor fibres as it were sticking out. For the former makes the bandaging uneven, and things sticking out do not let the turns be made easily. When tearing the bandages, one must not tear them across, by a transverse cut to the selvage, but straight, as it is woven, aiming to follow the warp straight. For along this the cloths tear easily, but along the weft the reverse; and besides, when torn in line with the warp they are stronger for the placing of the bandaged parts.

Of bandagings, as I said before, some are simple, others elaborate. And of these some have got their name from the parts being bandaged, some from an accidental feature, others by metaphor from a resemblance to animals. From the places bandaged, then: eye, nose, *boubōniskos* (groin-bandage) and those like them; from animals: crab, hawk, ram, hare, tortoise; from accidental features, such as the paling, both the yoked and the unyoked, the coverings, the chains and those like them. Of these bandagings, some are bandagings and nothing else, such as the dome, the royal, the little bowl, the separation. Others are bandagings and at the same time nooses, such as the hare with ears and the little herdsman and those like them. Further, of bandagings some are applied from one head, some from two, some from one and two heads. Further, of bandagings some are proper to certain parts and do not suit others, while others are common to other parts too. Further, of bandages some are visible in front, showing only the front parts of the person bandaged, some visible behind, others equally visible, showing equally both the front and the back parts, and these partly of the same kind, partly different in appearance. These things will be clear when the individual bandagings are shown.

It is worth first considering whether one should make the first laying-on of the bandages at random, and this must be investigated. For all those before us defined certain places of the body on which the heads must be placed, as when the head is bandaged. For whatever reason, they set the head [of the bandage] at the occiput, and leading the turns from there they complete the bandagings, giving no thought to the affection for which they bandage, whether they do this very thing suitably or not. And for the other parts too they somehow laid down definitions, doing this, it seems, either from want of learning or from ignorance. For the one who bandages correctly must try not only, as Hippocrates says, to make the kind suited to the form, but also to the affection of the person bandaged. Therefore we too place the heads not at random but where they must go; and the ends of the bandagings must also be placed, as the old man says. 'Moving parts such as joints: where they bend, put on as little and as neatly as possible, as at the hollow of the knee; where they are stretched, simple and broad, as at the kneecap. Put on additional turns for securing the parts around these, and for supporting the whole bandage, in the unmoving and slacker parts of the body, such as above and below the knee. It agrees [with this that for] the shoulder the turn [goes] around the other armpit, for the groin around the other flank, and for the shin above the calf. For those where the escape is upward, the hold is from below; for those where it is downward, the opposite; and for those where there is none, such as the head, make the securing turns on the most even part, and use the bandage as little obliquely as possible, so that the most stable [turn], put on last, holds the most shifting ones.' It befits one to bandage well, aiming also at the numbers concerning the operation. For since there are two kinds of operation, as Hippocrates says, one in which we are completing, the other in which we have completed, in both one must take care, while bandaging, to work quickly, painlessly, readily, with good rhythm: quickly, with the aim of accomplishing the works; painlessly, to act with ease; readily, prepared for everything; with good rhythm, to be done pleasantly. And having bandaged, [the bandaging must] have all the excellences mentioned before: well and finely, and the rest.

On the proper use of bandaged parts, one must know the following. Some bandagings serve certain treatments and are taken up for the sake of holding together; others are taken up not for this but to do the work themselves, and these are entrusted with the cure. With these one must above all have determined exactly where the head should be placed, from where the turns should be made, and where one should finish. It is not possible to hand down the exact detail of each of these in writing, but it is possible to give starting points, through which the physician will be able to reason in particular cases, knowing the nature of each of the parts and how it is suited to bandaging, to support and to placing. He must know too what bandaging can do. Bandaging, then, can bring separated parts back into contact, draw together parts that are turned outward, straighten parts that are twisted, and do the opposite of all these. To bandage separated parts, such as those that are raised: the bandage must touch the base, that is, the seated parts from which they have separated, even if they are raised up. It must not press, and it must begin from the healthy part and finish at the wound, so that what lies beneath is drawn out, that is, squeezed out, and nothing further collects. Where we wish to separate parts, one must do everything opposite to what is done for parts being drawn together. Where parts are spread out, that is, turned outward, and we wish to draw them together from a distance, the rest must be done the same way, but the drawing together must be made from some distance and the pressure applied gradually: least at first, then more and more, the limit of the increase being that the parts touch and fit together, not that they are forced. Where parts that have been drawn together must be set apart, with inflammation use gentleness; without inflammation, the same preparation but the opposite bandaging. To straighten twisted parts, the rest is the same, but the parts that have moved away must be brought back, and the opposite parts in the opposite way. Knowing and keeping all these like laws, one must choose for each affection what fits it, without attending to set places. We for the present, in bandaging, define from where the turn must begin; for it was not easy to state each case worked out one by one in writing. For the sake of clear teaching we define, in handing down the bandages, the places from which one must begin, but in actual practice it is fitting to choose what suits the case.

Taking a cloth of suitable size, we tear it into six tails, leaving the middle whole, and lay this on the crown. Taking hold of the middle ones of the tails that hang down, we tear through the part lying over the ears and, placing the heads under the chin, we tie them. Placing the middle of another narrow strip on the nape and bringing the ends round over the forehead, we tie them at the sides of the head. Bringing the remaining four heads in this way, we fasten the back ones near the knot of the narrow strip, and the front ones by the nape. It is also possible, without knots, to tuck some under and put others over, pinning the last one.

We divide the cloth into four tails, leaving the middle whole, and lay this on the forehead. We take the front heads away to the nape, over the back heads that hang down, and tie them there. Turning back the other two heads, we bring them to the crown and tie them under it. It is also possible to bring those taken to the crown under the chin and tie them. We also use this on the nape, tying the heads at the sides of the head.

Dividing the cloth into eight tails, the middle being left untorn, of a size to cover the whole head, we lay it on the whole head; and of the tails hanging down we bring two to the chin, cutting through their continuity at the ears, and tie them there. Four remaining behind and two in front, we bring the last of the back ones up over the others to the forehead, and tuck one under at the end, and lay the other over to secure what lies beneath. Then in this way we bring the front tails to the nape. Likewise, securing the first heads with these and tucking one of them under the other, we bring the other two back ones to the forehead, tucking one under, bringing the other over, and pinning the last one at the sides of the head. With the torn bandage that binds the head without knots we guard against the pressure caused by knots.

The middle of the heads [lies] over the whole head; let four hang straight down over the forehead and the other four over the nape. Of those over the forehead, let the two outer ones, once torn, be taken to the nape and tied there; and let these from the nape be brought to the ones over the forehead and tied in turn. Then next let the remaining two over the forehead, torn, be brought to the nape, and those from the nape to the forehead.

It suits cases where we wish to cover the whole head; it was called a covering. The holder is a very long band placed over the covering lengthwise in a circle round the face and the head to secure the covering; the draw-down is made from a long band. It is used to draw the bandage down so that it does not slip off, and it is done thus. Let a cloth be taken so wide as to cover the whole head, and in length as long as possible, or able to do this when doubled. Let one head of it be placed on the nape, and let the other hang down over the face. Let the middle of a narrow strip be placed under the chin, and let the heads be brought over the cheeks and over the sinciput, where, having been crossed, let them be brought to the chin(?). Let the middle of another narrow strip [be placed] on the forehead and the heads [brought] round to the nape, and there let them be tied to each other and to the heads of the draw-down. Let the part hanging over the face be divided straight into two tails as far as between the eyebrows, and, once split, be taken round over the forehead to the nape and tied there. It is also possible to make both the holder and the draw-down from one longer band in this way: the middle on the sinciput, the heads straight down over the cheeks under the chin; then under the lobes of the ears to the nape. There let them cross, from the nape to the forehead, and the knot at the sides of the head. Simple bandages.

So it remains to speak also of the elaborate ones, first making clear that of the turns one is called straight, another transverse, another oblique, as the names indicate; another the crown turn, another the forehead turn, another the cheek turn, another the chin turn, another the well-rounded, another circular bandaging, another the adze. The crown turn, then, is the one brought over the sinciput like wreaths; the forehead turn the one circled round the forehead; the chin turn the one over the chin. Likewise the cheek turn [is named] from the part; and the adze is the one that is hollow on one side, being of a single form, and convex on the other. These, then, are the names of the courses.

This bandaging suits, according to some, separations at the sutures; according to others, cases where there is a wound and the adjacent parts have come away, for gluing them together and, because the wound is covered, for the discharge of the fluids. It is done thus: the head of the strip is set at the side of the head, then it is brought obliquely to the crown and one temple. From there a cheek turn is completed; and another cheek turn, oblique, opposite the first, so that a crossing is formed at the nape; from the nape an oblique one, apart from the first ones; then two cheek turns and again an oblique one are made, so that a rhombus forms in the middle; then forehead turns over the same, to cover the bare parts.

It suits the same cases as the dome. It is done thus: the head of the strip is set under the nape, then the roll is brought under the lobe of the ear, then obliquely to the sinciput and to the nape; from the nape obliquely to the sinciput, opposite the first, then under the lobe of the ear, then to the nape, and from there a forehead turn is completed, so that the middle is a half-rhombus. The end, both in this and in all the bandagings, should be held with pins at the sides of the head. It is possible, from the first, to make the turns not from below upward but the reverse, if it suits.

It suits cases where we wish to bandage the crown and sinciput together. It is done thus: having set [the head] at the nape, we bring the roll in a straight line over the crown to the forehead, and holding it there with the index finger of our left hand, we bring it back again to the nape parallel to the first; and from the nape we bring a third [course] to the forehead, parallel. Then, having wound over the band held by the finger, we complete a forehead turn.

It is suitable for the same cases as the dome. Besides its usefulness it has a certain elegance. When the dome has been completed, one must set the head of a narrow strip under the turns at the nape, and from there bring it obliquely over the crown to the sinciput. At the forehead the loop of the first band will be wound under the [turns] at the forehead; then bring it obliquely to the sinciput, crown, nape. From the nape to the lobe of the right ear, and to the sinciput, and to the lobe of the left ear, and to the nape. To this bandaging we add a forehead turn for security.

When the dome has been completed, we set the head of a strip a finger wide, or still narrower, at the nape and bring the roll in a straight line to the crown, the middle of the sinciput and the forehead; and having folded it at the forehead, we bring it back again over the same [course] to the nape. From the nape, shifting to the right side of the head, we bring it past the crown to the sinciput and the left temple; and having doubled the band at the temple, we bring the roll over the oblique [course] already laid on to the right side of the head; and from there, likewise bending it back, we bring it again to the temple, and we do this three times, so that at the temple three loops, bent back in overlapping fashion, give the appearance of curls. And after it has come for the third time to the right side of the nape, shift it to the left, so that the same is done at the other temple too; and after all we complete a forehead turn to hold the turns together.

It suits the same cases as the dome of Glaucias. It is done thus: leaving a moderate part of the band over the face, bring the roll to the sinciput, to the crown, the nape, and there, having told an assistant to hold it, shift the roll and give a forehead turn; then, in this way, bring the head left hanging over the face up over the first [course] to the sinciput, crown, nape, and secure it at the nape.

It suits all cases where, through chronic flux of the eyes, [the scalp] has been scalped, for drawing together the separated parts, and also those who for some other cause have a wound above the forehead. It is done thus: having set the head of the bandage at the nape, we bring the rest under the lobe of either the right ear or the other, whichever we judge it better to turn over first. From the ear to the adjacent temple, transversely to the sinciput, then to the other temple, under the lobe of the ear, then to the nape; from the nape, pressing down the head laid on, we make the turn to the ear, to the forehead, so that the turn of the first over the sinciput is lowest, both being marked inward, opposite to each other, and the further turns over the same. Another is also done from two crown turns, one running below the cut, the other marked above it, each inward; and the further turns of the lower one go upward, and those of the upper one toward the lower.

It is suitable for cases where we wish to bandage the sinciput and the parts adjacent to it together. It is done thus: on the so-called half-rhombus, made without the forehead turn, we bring the turn from the nape past the crown obliquely to the forehead. Bending the band at the forehead in a crescent, so that its concave side faces upward and its convex side looks toward the space between the brows, we bring it to the parts opposite the crown and to the nape, and so we add the forehead turn. This bandaging, with the usefulness that the hare provides, is somewhat more seemly.
It suits the same cases as the *spenkranis* also. But it is much more secure; for after the *spenkranis* the hare without ears is woven on, so that we need not say more.

It suits the same cases as the masterless Thais, I mean the sinciput and the neighbouring places. It is done thus: leaving a fair part of the band hanging over the face, draw the roll over the sinciput straight as if toward the nape, and from there, shifting, bring it under the lobe of the ear; to the sinciput and obliquely to the nape; from the nape obliquely to the opposite parts and to the sinciput, temple, under the lobe of the ear, then to the nape; then, bringing up the head left hanging over the face, fold it at the forehead three times in overlapping fashion, so that [the folds] lie on one another like steps, and so bring the forehead turn over them along it.

It suits cases where we wish to bandage the jaw on one side, whether for a wound or a dislocation or the so-called canine spasm or something else. The head at the nape, obliquely to the crown and sinciput, temple, cheek turns; then under the chin and the lobe of the opposite ear to the nape; from the nape to the chin, lobes of the ears, and after the chin turn to the nape, and the further turns over the same. So, if it is better to bandage from above downward; but it is also done from below upward thus: the head at the nape, the roll under the lobe of the ear, under the chin; then a cheek turn, then an oblique one to the sinciput, nape, then a chin turn and a forehead turn.

This is found suitable for cases where on both sides of the jaw there are dislocations or anything else of those stated for the one-sided [bandage]. The head at the nape, obliquely to the crown, sinciput, and a cheek turn under the chin; then a cheek turn lying opposite on the jaws, and to the sinciput over the one laid on, until a crossing is formed; then to the nape and under the lobe of the ear, chin, to the nape, and a forehead turn.

The head under the nape, [below the lobe] of the ear and under the chin, then a cheek turn and an oblique one past the crown to the nape, under the lobe of the opposite ear, under the chin; then a cheek turn, then an oblique one over the sinciput to the nape, then a forehead turn.

Let the middle be placed on the nape, [and] the rolls from the crown obliquely to the sinciput, so that a crossing is formed on it; then to the cheeks, under the chin, under the lobes of the ears, to the nape; from the nape in a circle to the forehead and nape; then a chin turn and a forehead turn, and the further turns over the same.

The middle at the forehead, the rolls to the nape, and a crossing on it; then under the lobes of the ears, under the chin, then cheek turns and to the sinciput, obliquely to the nape, then a chin turn and forehead turns.
The middle at the nape. The heads under the lobes of the ears, under the chin, then a cheek turn, and the rest like the preceding one.

The head at the nape, the roll under the lobe of the ear to the temple. Over the sinciput obliquely to the nape and a forehead turn, and the further turns over the same, several times. Let it be bandaged thus from below upward, or from above. If it is better to bandage thus: the head at the nape, obliquely to the crown, sinciput and temple, under the lobe of the ear to the nape, and a forehead turn.

The head at the nape. The roll under the lobe of the ear to the temple and sinciput, obliquely to the nape, and a forehead turn toward the outer corner of the eye and to the sinciput. Obliquely to the nape; from the nape obliquely to the sinciput, opposite the one before it, crossing at the sinciput; then under the lobe of the ear to the nape, and a forehead turn.
The middle at the nape. The heads to the crown, sinciput, making a crossing on it; then under the lobes of the ears to the nape, then a forehead turn.
The middle at the nape. The heads under the lobes of the ears to the outer corners of the eyes; then to the sinciput and nape, then a forehead turn; some also add a chin turn.
Having bandaged the straight two-sided halter without the chin turn, at the end we bring it to the bridge of the nose, then to the nape, and add a crown turn.
Likewise, on the yoked-back [bandage] when it has been applied, we also add the chin turn.

This suits those who have wounds on many parts of the head and the cheeks. Bandage the oblique two-sided halter together [with it], and after this also the *skaphion* of Glaucias, and then the two-sided halters. Some, wishing [to be] more showy, prepare a *kephalos* and sew it on. The same is also done otherwise, without the oblique halter and the chin turns.

Leaving a fair part of the band to hang over the face, draw the roll straight to the nape, and from there bandage the straight halter until it covers the whole cheek and the head; and at the end, bending back the head left hanging over the face, bring it in a straight line over the crown to the nape and secure it likewise, if you wish, adding the lobe.

The half-rhombus that has taken on the so-called ears is named thus. It is applied either for the sake of appearance in single combats, or for the sake of providing a hold on the head when some injury of the face is being treated. But if it is applied for the sake of appearance, these [ears] must be short and placed in the middle of the forehead, for so it would preserve its likeness to the animal; but if for a hold, [they must be] large, so that someone grasping [them] with crooked fingers can hold [them], and [placed] in the middle.

It is carried out thus: the loop called the herdsman's loop, or [the one made] with hooked bends, which we have often set out briefly in [the work] on loops, is placed on the forehead from one part of the bandage, and on it is completed the half-rhombus, also called the *plinthion* (little brick).
Head at the nape. The roll [goes] to the crown, to the sinciput, the middle of the brows, the eye, so as to cover [it], then under the lobe of the ear and to the nape, then the forehead turn.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] to the crown, sinciput, middle of the brows, to the eye; then, I think, [one should] draw it along under the lobe of the ear to the eye, to the sinciput, to the nape, then the forehead turn.

Head at the nape. The winding [goes] over the crown, sinciput, middle of the brows, to the eye; then under the lobe of the opposite ear to the other eye, middle of the brows, sinciput and to the nape, then the forehead turn. It is also possible, reversing the first, to bandage the patient from below upwards, if this is of benefit.

Middle at the nape. The heads [go] to the crown, to the sinciput, the middle of the brows, and cross at this very point; then to the eyes and under the lobes of the ears, to the nape, and the forehead turn.
Middle at the forehead. The heads [go] to the nape, crossed from the nape, and [the rest] likewise to the bandaging before this one.
Head at the nape. The roll [goes] to the crown, sinciput, eye, straight to the corner of the mouth, under the chin and the lobe of the ear, to the nape, and the forehead turn.

Before the forehead turn: from the nape another [turn] is brought to the other, opposite eye, and straight to the corner of the mouth, under the chin, to the other eye and to the opposite lobe, to the nape, and the forehead turn.

Head below the nape. The winding [goes] under the lobe of the ear, then under the chin to the corner of the mouth, the eye, to the sinciput and to the nape; then under the lobe and under the chin to the opposite corner of the mouth, the eye, the middle of the brows, and a crossing there; then under the sinciput and the nape, then the forehead turn.
Likewise to the oblique one, the middle being placed at the nape and the heads being brought either from above or from below; but the middle is placed under the chin.

Each strip [is] in breadth as much as will cover the nose, and in length such that, doubled, it can reach from the nose straight to the nape. We place the head at the nape, and bring the rest straight over the crown, the sinciput, [to] the ridge of the nose. The rest [is] left hanging over the face, and this we split straight into two legs as far as the upper lip. Then, in the same way, we place the middle of another narrow strip, but a longer one, under the tip of the nose and over the legs hanging over the face. And we bring the heads under the lobes of the ears, below the nape, making a crossing over the one put on before; and handing [them] to an assistant, we next bring the legs over the face, bending them back on either side of the nose to the middle of the brows, so that a crossing is made there, and the heads obliquely over the crown to the nape; and fastening [them] at the same end, we bring on the heads held by the assistant [and] complete forehead turns, the ends being taken up [and tied] to each other with a knot, or as with a pin, at the sides of the head.

We split the cloth into four legs, leaving the middle continuous, and placing this under the tip [of the nose], we let the upper [legs] hang down, and the lower ones we bring first to the cheekbones and the outer corners of the eyes, to the sinciput, and having crossed [them] we tell an assistant to hold [them]. The other two heads, having crossed [them] under the lobes at the nape, [we bring] around to the forehead, and, taking [them] up at the side of the head and bringing the held [heads] to the nape, we secure [them].

One middle under the tip [of the nose]; let its heads [go] to the outer corners of the eyes, to the sinciput, and having been crossed be held. Another middle under the tip of the nose; its heads are both [brought] under the lobes and knotted at the nape. A third middle at the forehead; its heads [go] around the head, and the knot at the side of the head.

One middle under the tip [of the nose]; let its heads [go] to the outer corners of the eyes, to the sinciput, and having been crossed be likewise held. The second middle above the tip; its heads under the lobes, to the nape, crossed from the nape around the head, circling to the forehead, and the knot at the sides of the head.

With one [strip] laid straight along the nose, we leave half of it hanging over the forehead in front, and the half hanging over the face we take straight over the crown to the nape. Placing the middle of the other under the tip [of the nose], we bring the heads under the lobes of the ears and to the nape. Having crossed [them] at the nape, we then bend back the [half] hanging over the face over the one put on before, and take it straight to the crown and the nape. And securing the heads with those crossed at the nape, we complete a forehead turn.

Let the middle of one [strip] be under the tip [of the nose]; let its heads [go] from the sides of the nose to the middle of the brows, where, having been crossed, let them be taken straight along the crown to the nape, and there held. The middle of the second [is] above the tip of the nose; let its heads [go] under the lobes of the ears to the nape, and there be knotted to each other and to the held ones. The middle of the third at the forehead; its heads around the head, and the knot at the side of the head.

With the first band arranged likewise, and the second again likewise, one brings the heads of the second to the nape, crosses them, and completes forehead turns with them, the heads of the first strip being either caught under them or themselves also crossed at the nape; then, being brought under the chin, we knot [them] there.

Leaving a fair part of the bandage to hang over the face, as much as will be enough to reach to the nape, we then bring the roll straight over the nose, the middle of the brows, the sinciput, the crown, to the nape; bending it from the nape to the lobe of the opposite ear; holding the roll at the nape, we bend back the head left hanging over the face and bring it straight over the first [turn], over the crown and nape, and securing [it] we bring the roll round to the forehead; then to the nape, and at the side of the head we secure the roll.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] obliquely to the crown and the sinciput, the small corner of the eye, to the cheekbones; then under the tip of the nose and to the opposite cheekbone, past the outer corner of the eye, to the sinciput, to the crown, opposite to the first, to the nape; from the nape to the lobe of the opposite ear and to the nape; from the nape the forehead turn.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] obliquely along the crown to the temple and the outer corner of the eye, under the tip of the nose and under the lobe of the ear; then to the nape. Bending the head from the nape, we bring it opposite to the first, obliquely to the temple, under the tip of the nose and under the lobe of the opposite ear, to the nape; from the nape to the lobe of the ear, over the tip of the nose and under the lobe of the ear, then to the nape; from the nape we add the forehead turn.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] obliquely to the crown, sinciput, middle of the brows, then from the side of the nose past the large corner of the eye straight to the adjacent wing of the nose, to the corner of the mouth, then under the chin and under the lobe of the ear to the nape; from the nape obliquely along the crown and to the sinciput, opposite to the first, to the middle of the brows, so that a crossing is made there, and from the side of the nose, opposite to the first, to the corner of the mouth; then under the chin and under the lobe of the opposite ear, then to the nape; from the nape the forehead turn, and [one] under the ridge of the nose; then under the lobe of the opposite ear and to the nape. To this bandaging some also add a chin turn; it suits cases where we wish to bandage the middle of the brows and the ridge of the nose together.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] obliquely along the crown, sinciput, to the middle of the brows, past the large corner of the eye, to the cheekbone, under the lobe of the ear; to the nape; opposite to the first, so that a crossing is made at the middle of the brows, and obliquely along the sinciput and crown to the nape; from the nape to the lobe of the ear; under the ridge of the nose and to the opposite lobe of the ear, then to the nape; from the nape the forehead turn. To this bandaging some also add a crown turn for the sake of appearance; it can also be applied from two heads, if need requires. It suits the same cases as the one before it.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] straight over the crown to the middle of the brows, past the large corner of the eye, from the side of the nose to the very tip of the nose, and past that of the other large corner of the eye to the middle of the brows, so that a crossing is made at the middle of the brows; straight, alongside the first, to the crown and nape. Bending [it] from the nape, we bring the roll to the lobe of the ear, to the tip of the nose and the opposite lobe of the ear, to the nape; from the nape the forehead turn. It is also possible to add a crown turn. To this bandaging some, for the sake of appearance, add the so-called half-rhombus, whose execution we have already described.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] straight to the crown, sinciput, middle of the brows, large corner of the eye, from the side of the nose under the tip, then under the lobe of the opposite ear, and over the tip of the nose, then likewise under the lobe of the ear, to the nape; from the nape the forehead turn.

It suits the same cases as the bandaging before it. It is carried out thus: smearing with glue or gum one end of a rather long [strip of] red leather, we glue it to the nose on the side toward which it is twisted, and we lead the other end under the lobe of the ear to the nape, from the nape to the forehead, where we glue it on the forehead in the same way.

Middle over the ear. The heads below the ear being crossed, one [goes] to the forehead, the other to the crown, to the nape; from the nape let the one from the forehead be led over the crossing, the other along the crown to the forehead, and let them be knotted at the side; and the lower heads being crossed, one under the chin, the other behind the nape, let them be knotted there too.

Let the head of the bandage be placed near the nape, behind the affected ear; let the turn be made over it, so that the ear is partly covered, and let the roll be brought up to the sinciput near the forehead and along the front near the opposite ear; then under the chin and over the ear to the sinciput and the back of the opposite ear, and under the chin and the lobe of the ear to the nape, and from the nape to the forehead and to the nape.

Head at the nape; the winding [goes] under the lobe of the unaffected ear to the sinciput and the front of the affected ear, and under the chin; from the chin under the lobe of the ear and to the nape; from the nape obliquely over the ear, then the forehead turn.

The middle of the bandaging [is placed] over the part bandaged, with some of the heads let down along the neck, others upward as toward the head; of these let the front ones be knotted at the sinciput, the middle ones at the crown, both to one another and to those at the sinciput; and let the back ones, led to the nape, be crossed, and, arranged in a circle round the head and forehead, be knotted at the side of the head.

The middle of one [strip] at the sinciput. The heads [go] along the cheeks under the chin; from the chin along the cheeks, parallel to the first, to the sinciput, and let it be knotted there. If we wish to bandage the eyes, let them be led not alongside the first ones but over the eyes, then to the sinciput, and, crossed, let them be led to the nape. The middle of a second strip at the sinciput, and let the heads [go] past the outer corners of the eyes to the chin and be knotted there. The middle of a third at the ridge of the nose; the heads [go] under the lobes to the nape and, crossed, round to the forehead, and the knot at the side of the head.
Head at the nape, straight to the forehead and the middle of the brows; then to the nape; from the nape the forehead turn. It is also done from two heads.

We place the middle, which is also continuous, on the lower lip. Of the heads, we lead the upper ones to the chin, from the chin to the nape, and from the nape, crossing them, along the crown and sinciput; and having ordered them to be held there, we lead the remaining two heads [under] the lobes to the chin and, crossing them, to the forehead, and we secure them together with those being held.

Middle over it. Let the lower heads, [led] past the outer corners of the eyes to the sinciput and crossed, be led off to the nape. Let the other heads [go] under the lobes of the ears to the nape and, crossed, to the forehead, and be fastened to one another.
The head at the nape. The roll [goes] under the lobe of the ear to the lower lip and under the lobe to the nape.
The middle over the lip; the heads under the lobes to the nape, and the forehead turn.

Head at the nape. The roll [goes] by the lobe of the ear to the lip and the opposite lobe to the nape; from the nape along the crown and obliquely to the sinciput, the temple, then the cheek turn under the chin, and the opposite cheek turn to the sinciput, so that a crossing is made there, then to the nape and the forehead turn.

Head at the nape; the roll [goes] obliquely to the sinciput, past the outer corner of the eye to the upper lip, then to the opposite temple and the outer corner of the eye to the sinciput, opposite to the one before, making a crossing at the sinciput too, then to the nape and the forehead turn.

The middle over the upper lip; the heads [go] past the temples and the adjacent corners of the eyes to the sinciput, and with a crossing there to the nape; from the nape both the forehead turn and to the nape.

The middle at the nape. The lower heads [go] onto the cheeks past the outer corners of the eyes to the sinciput and are knotted there; the others under the lobes to the nape, crossed from the nape. If they are rather short, they are fastened at the nape to the first ones; if rather long, the forehead turns are also added. Having finished the bandagings, simple and elaborate, suited to the head and face, let us pass on to those that follow.

It is named from the resemblance to ears of grain produced by the turns. It is useful both for a broken collarbone and for a dislocated upper arm. It is carried out in this way: rolling up soft wool, we place it in the armpit of the part to be bandaged, making a filling for the hollow; then, placing the head of a rolled bandage, of width and length proportioned to the part bandaged, at the unaffected armpit, we lead the winding obliquely across the back; then past the point of the shoulder under the armpit of the affected arm, then to the point of the shoulder, so that a crossing is made there; then obliquely across the chest under the unaffected armpit; from the armpit obliquely across the back to the collarbone, so that some parts of the second turn fall on parts of the one laid before; from the collarbone under the armpit and to the collarbone, so that a second crossing is made, then the unaffected armpit; and the turns [go] over the same [places].

When the spica has been completed, the middle of another strip [is placed] under the forearm, held bent at a right angle. The heads [go] straight to the point of the shoulder, and, crossed there, obliquely to the unaffected armpit, then round the ribs and the affected arm until they cover the whole, and the ends at the unaffected armpit.

The middle under the armpit of the affected arm; let the heads, crossed at the point of the shoulder, be led off obliquely, one across the back, the other across the chest, under the unaffected armpit; and the turns likewise.

It suits the same cases as the spica. It is carried out thus: after bandaging the spica, one must wind one circular [turn] round the upper arm; from the upper arm, having completed the winding, lead it obliquely to the unaffected armpit and secure it there.

It suits also the cases for which the crane [is used]. It is carried out thus: having first bandaged the spica, we lead one turn from the point of the shoulder straight to the forearm held at a right angle, and from there straight again to the point of the shoulder; from the point of the shoulder obliquely to the unaffected armpit; then a circular [turn] round the upper arm and ribs to the armpit, and there we secure the end.

The middle over the affected shoulder; the heads [go] straight down to the forearm near the elbow, vertically; again, parallel to the first, to the point of the shoulder; from the point of the shoulder under the unaffected armpit, then circular [turns].

The middle under the unaffected armpit. The heads [go] round the ribs and the upper arm, round again to the unaffected armpit; from the armpit obliquely to the affected shoulder point; from the shoulder point vertically along the upper arm to the elbow, and again from the elbow to the shoulder point; from the shoulder point to the unaffected armpit, then round the upper arm.

It suits those who have an injury at both shoulders. It is carried out thus: when the simple spica has been completed, after [the turn] has reached the armpit of the bandaged arm, we next lead it obliquely to the other arm and its shoulder point, so that a crossing is made there; then the opposite armpit; and the turns [go] over the same [places].

It is named simply thus from its being similar to the corselets among the Romans which they call *cataphractae* (armoured cuirasses). It is suitable for cases where we wish to bandage the parts around the collarbones and the shoulder blade, or the breastbone, or the upper back, or the ribs. The bandaging is in some respect similar to the double spica. It is carried out thus: the head under the armpit; the winding obliquely in front over the breastbone near the junction of the collarbones with the xiphoid [process], and alongside the neck to the shoulder blade of the opposite arm; then under the adjacent armpit; from the armpit to the neck over the first [turn], so that a crossing is made near the neck, and obliquely over the opposite shoulder blade; then under the armpit; from the armpit alongside the neck to the vertebra of the neck, so that a crossing is made over it; then under the armpit and obliquely near the junction of the collarbones, so that here too a crossing is made; and alongside the neck to the shoulder blade and to the armpit, so that four crossings are made: one in front, one behind, and two over the collarbones. The turns [go] over the same [places], [ending] in circular [turns] round the chest and ribs, so that the whole bandaging becomes similar to a corselet.

The middle under the armpit. Let the heads be crossed over the adjacent collarbone near the neck; then obliquely under the opposite armpit; from the armpit to the adjacent collarbone, and over it a crossing near the neck, and obliquely to the opposite armpit; then circular [turns] round the chest.

This bandaging is suitable for cases where we wish to bandage the breastbone or the upper back or the ribs or the chest. Placing the middle of two strips of suitable size over the shoulders, we let the heads hang straight down. Then, having bandaged with a rolled bandage in a circle both the whole chest and the ribs so as to cover [them], securing the end, [and] attaching the heads that were let hang down, behind and in front, to the circular [turns], and if they are rather long, bending them back up to the point of the shoulder, we secure them further.
The strips mentioned before do not hang straight, but obliquely, so that a crossing is made over the nape and the upper back; and the rest is completed in the same way as the vertical [one].

It suits the same cases as the *maschalistēr* (armpit bandage). It is carried out thus: having closed the corselet with two heads, after throwing many circular turns round the chest, so as to cover [it] as far as the navel, we then knot the heads to each other, making the 'wolf' loop; and leading the remainders of the heads to the right and left flank, we tuck them under the circular turns, letting the ends hang down, about four fingers in length, so that their appearance becomes like the fringes of a corselet.

The head over the right flank. The knot obliquely to the ribs, breastbone, shoulder; then under the shoulder, so that a crossing is made over it; then obliquely over the upper back to the flank, over the head laid on beforehand; then circular [turns] round the belly to the left flank, and from there obliquely over the upper back, so that a crossing is made over it, and to the right shoulder; then under the armpit and to the shoulder, so that a crossing is made over it, and obliquely over the breastbone and ribs to the left flank; then a circular [turn]; and the turns [go] over the same [places], so as to cover everything that needs the bandaging.
Having further bandaged the crossed corselet, next with a narrow strip wind one or even a second circular [turn] round over the breastbone and upper back, and secure the end with a pin.

It suits the same cases as the *cataphractēs* (corselet). It is carried out thus: the head over the upper back; the roll obliquely to the shoulder blade, the point of the shoulder, under the armpit, then to the point of the shoulder, so that a crossing is made over it; and obliquely over the breasts to the navel; from the navel, turning back, we lead it to the opposite breast, obliquely to the point of the shoulder, so that a crossing is made over it; then to the upper back; then in circular [turns] round the ribs; and the turns [go] over the same [places].

It suits cases where we wish to bandage the upper back. It is carried out thus: the head over the flank, say the left; the winding over the upper back to the right shoulder and to the armpit; from the armpit to the left shoulder blade; then under the armpit and to the shoulder; from the shoulder obliquely over the upper back, opposite to the first; then circular round the flanks once and a second time, and the same [turn] takes up the end. This can also be made visible in front, if one arranges the same turns not behind but in front.

It suits the same cases as the one before it. Taking a strip of suitable length and width, we slit it in the middle so that the head passes through. We let the ends hang down, one over the back, the other over the abdomen, and we weave on the so-called crossed corselet; and slitting the ends of the strip laid underneath beforehand, we let them hang down at the end.

It suits cases where we wish to bandage one side of the neck. The head at the middle of the side; the winding obliquely over the upper back to the neck and the breastbone; then to the side, over the head laid on beforehand, and a circular [turn] round the chest.

The head under the armpit. The winding obliquely over the upper back to the neck and to the breastbone, armpit, and to the opposite armpit, and obliquely to the breastbone and neck, so that a crossing is made over it, and obliquely over the upper back under the armpit, circular. The turns [go] over the same [places].

Two strips, two fingers in width, of suitable length: placing their middles over the shoulders, [we bring] the heads to the navel, and the others, crossing them over the back, we pin to them; then we weave on the so-called basket-shaped crane.
It suits the same cases as the one before this. It is made up of the double *trachēlistēr* (neck bandage) with the basket-shaped crane carried out in addition.

The head over the flank. The turn obliquely over the collarbone to the shoulder blade, then under the armpit and to the collarbone, so that a crossing is made above the point of the shoulder; then transversely to the back of the neck and to the opposite collarbone, under the armpit and to the collarbone, so that a crossing is made here too, and obliquely beside the breast to the opposite flank, so that a crossing is also made over the breastbone; then circular [turns] round the flanks; then obliquely round the upper back and to the point of the shoulder, armpit, then to the point of the shoulder; then transversely in front over the junction of the collarbones and to the point of the shoulder, and obliquely over the upper back to the flank; then a circular [turn]. Woven on to it is either the double crane or the crossed neck bandage or the one called double.

It suits cases where we wish to bandage also the part below the breastbone and back. It is made from the 'arrowhead' and the 'star', the ends, which in the arrowhead were pinned to each other at the flanks, being led along and hanging down there.
Having first secured over the shoulders the strips which we showed for the arrowhead, add further a neck bandage in two [parts], which is double, then the basket-shaped crane.

The bandaging is showy, since when completed it becomes similar to the right angles of little altars: with the basket-shaped neck bandage applied first, and with the crane of the same shape, the vertical breast-bandage of Sostratus with its slings is added.
This too is showy; it suits the same cases, when we further bandage once again with the vertical breast-bandage of Sostratus, which some call the 'fourth'.
Placing two strips over the back as for the vertical breast-bandage, we weave on the simple rhombus.

The head over the side. The winding obliquely over the breastbone to the point of the shoulder, then transversely over the back of the neck to the opposite point of the shoulder, and under the armpit from front to back, and to the same point of the shoulder, and obliquely to the breastbone, then circular over the flank. The same becomes visible behind when we interchange, making the front turns behind and the back ones in front.

It suits cases where the ribs are bandaged. It is made up thus: the middle of the bandage over the back of the neck; the heads obliquely over the breastbone, hooked into each other, under the armpits to the upper back, and there, hooked again, let them be led off, and so on until the whole chest is bandaged, let them be hooked now behind, now in front. Let the ends be knotted to each other. Charioteers use this bandaging to hold the ribs together. Having finished also the bandagings for the chest, let us speak of the next ones.

It suits the groin. It is carried out thus: the head over the flank, the opposite turn obliquely over the buttock near the affected groin, then to the perineum from below upwards and obliquely to the groin, then circular over the hip and over the flank, over the head laid on beforehand; and the turns [go] from below upwards over them.

The head over the abdomen; the winding obliquely to the hip socket, beside the perineum to the groin from below upwards, over the [head] laid on beforehand, to the hip and groin, beside the perineum and hip socket from below upwards, and to the lower belly; and the turns [go] over the same [places], so that both groins are covered.

The middle over the groin. The heads [go] to the hip socket and are crossed there: one over the groin, the other on the outside. Then let them be led up over the same [place], and the turns [go] over the same [places].

Of the shorter head, about two or three hand-breadths are left hanging over the groin. The winding is led over the flank to the hip and the abdomen, then obliquely to the hip socket and the groin from below upwards, and to the flank and the hip and the opposite flank and the abdomen, when the head left hanging is bent back up onto the groin, so that a fold is made over it, or it is caught by the winding; then it is completed again at the groin, then to the hip and the abdomen, and again the first head is folded from above downwards and caught by the winding, and so the bandaging goes on until it is finished, the one always being folded, the other wound over [it]; and the end is pinned.

The middle of a band over the loins. The heads [go] over the groin, as in the single [bandage], leaving another bandage hanging. The heads over the abdomen, and a double *boubōniskos* (groin bandage) is completed, the little bands left hanging below being folded, as was said for the double [one].

The middle of a little band over the loins; the heads are knotted over the abdomen; then the head of a rolled bandage under the belt, the winding under the penis, then onto the belt from above downwards; then under the penis and around the belt; then it completes [it] under the testicles and under the belt.

After the band has been put round, the head of the bandage onto the penis, and circular turns around it until it is covered; then around the belt, then under the penis and around the belt, then under the testicles and onto the belt.

Taking a rag of suitable size, we split it into four legs, leaving the middle whole, and place it under the penis; and bringing up the heads, we slit those on the one side near the penis, and through this [slit] we pass the others through onto the belt.
